title: Hudson Enters the Harbor
text: Henry Hudson's Halve Maen enters the Upper Bay in September 1609. Forest covers Manhattan to the shore, and Lenape villages stand beside its creeks and ponds.

title: Lenape Manhattan
text: Bark-covered wigwams mark Werpoes above the Collect Pond, Rechtauck at Corlears Hook and the landing place Sapohanikan on the Hudson. The map draws them from Bolton's survey of Lenape sites.

title: Lenape Brooklyn
text: Marechkawick, the seat of the chieftaincy, stands near the East River shore, with villages at Werpos and Rinnegaconck close by. Woods and tidal marsh cover the rest of Kings County.

title: Manhattan Changes Hands
text: Director Peter Minuit acquires Manhattan from the Lenape for goods worth 60 guilders, as a letter of 5 November 1626 reports. The Dutch settlement lies at the island's southern tip.

title: Pavonia
text: A West India Company director buys the west bank of the North River from the Lenape - Hoboken, Ahasimus and Aressick - for a patroonship called Pavonia, opposite New Amsterdam.

title: Bronck's Land
text: Jonas Bronck settles on the mainland across the Harlem River; the river beside his farm, and later the borough, take his name.

title: Fort Amsterdam
text: Fort Amsterdam, begun in 1625, guards the southern tip of Manhattan; inside its walls stands the Church in the Fort, built in 1642. The Dutch West India Company's town grows around it.

title: Breuckelen
text: The village of Breuckelen on Long Island receives its own municipal government from the Dutch West India Company in 1646. It faces New Amsterdam across the East River.

title: The Wall
text: In spring 1653 New Amsterdam builds a palisade across the island against an English attack. The path along it becomes Wall Street.

title: Wyckoff House
text: The Pieter Claesen Wyckoff House in Flatlands dates from about 1652 and still stands, among the oldest surviving buildings in the state. Farmland of the Dutch towns of Kings County surrounds it.

title: Bergen
text: Stuyvesant orders a palisaded village laid out on the ridge behind Communipaw. Bergen, with its square and four gates, is the first permanent town in New Jersey.

title: New Amsterdam
text: Between the fort and the wall, the town's houses cluster along a few streets. The Stadt Huys, a former tavern, has been the city hall since 1653.

title: Oude Dorp
text: Dutch and French-speaking families found Oude Dorp near South Beach, the first lasting European settlement on Staten Island.

title: New Amsterdam Becomes New York
text: An English squadron under Richard Nicolls arrives at the end of August; Stuyvesant surrenders the town without a shot in early September and it is renamed for the Duke of York.

title: The Elizabethtown Purchase
text: Weeks after the English take New Netherland, men from Long Island buy the land between the Raritan and the Passaic from the Lenape. Elizabethtown becomes the first English town and the first capital of New Jersey.

title: Newark
text: Puritans from Milford, Branford and New Haven, led by Robert Treat, land on the Passaic and lay out a town along a broad street with a training place and a market place.

title: Conference House
text: The Billopp House stands on the southern tip of Staten Island, built about 1680. It later hosts the failed peace talks of 1776 between the British and a delegation of the Continental Congress.

title: The Counties
text: The Province of New York is divided into twelve counties, among them New York, Kings, Queens, Richmond and Westchester. Their boundaries still shape the five boroughs.

title: The Tappan Patent
text: Governor Dongan grants the valley of the Sparkill to sixteen Dutch families from Manhattan; Tappan becomes the seat of Orange County.

title: King's Bridge
text: A toll bridge owned by Frederick Philipse spans Spuyten Duyvil Creek, carrying the Boston Post Road from Manhattan to the mainland.

title: Philipsburg Manor
text: A royal charter makes Frederick Philipse lord of a manor that runs from Spuyten Duyvil to the Croton River, with tenant farms and mills at Yonkers and on the Pocantico.

title: Trinity Church
text: Trinity Church, built in 1698 at the head of Wall Street, serves the Church of England congregation of the English city. The palisade is down; its path remains as Wall Street.

title: Morris-Jumel Mansion
text: Roger Morris builds this Palladian villa on Harlem Heights in 1765. In 1776 George Washington uses it as his headquarters during the fight for New York.

title: Battle of Long Island
text: British and Hessian troops turn the American lines on the heights of Brooklyn in the largest battle of the war; Washington ferries his army to Manhattan two nights later.

title: The Great Fire of 1776
text: Six days after the British take the city a fire starting near Whitehall Slip burns between 400 and 1,000 buildings, up to a quarter of the town, including Trinity Church.

title: Capital of the United States
text: George Washington takes the oath of office at Federal Hall on Wall Street; New York is the national capital until 1790.

title: The Society for Useful Manufactures
text: Alexander Hamilton's Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures is chartered by New Jersey and chooses the Great Falls of the Passaic for a planned industrial city. Its raceways drive mills for 150 years.

title: The Town of Jersey
text: The Associates of the Jersey Company buy Paulus Hook and lay out a town opposite Manhattan, the beginning of Jersey City.

title: The Commissioners' Plan
text: The commissioners' map fixes a grid of twelve avenues and 155 cross streets over Manhattan north of Houston Street. Above the town the island is still mostly farms and woods.

title: The Collect Is Filled
text: The Collect Pond, once the town's fresh water and by now polluted, is drained through a canal and filled; the Five Points slum rises on the sinking ground.

title: Steam Ferry to Brooklyn
text: Fulton's steam ferry Nassau begins crossing between Manhattan and Brooklyn, opening Brooklyn Heights to commuters.

title: The Erie Canal
text: The Erie Canal opens in 1825 and the canal boat Seneca Chief reaches New York nine days later. The canal makes the city the port of the interior, and South Street becomes its waterfront.

title: City of Brooklyn
text: The village and town of Brooklyn are incorporated as a city, soon the third largest in the country.

title: The Great Fire of 1835
text: In a freezing gale a fire burns seventeen blocks and between 530 and 700 buildings east of Broad Street, including the Merchants' Exchange.

title: Croton Water
text: The city celebrates the Croton Aqueduct, which brings river water 41 miles to a receiving reservoir in the future Central Park and a distributing reservoir at 42nd Street.

title: High Bridge
text: The aqueduct bridge that carries Croton water over the Harlem River is completed; it is the oldest bridge standing in the city.

title: The Crystal Palace
text: The iron-and-glass hall of the Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations stands on Reservoir Square beside the Croton reservoir, with the Latting Observatory, a tall wooden tower, to its north.

title: Llewellyn Park
text: Llewellyn Haskell and the architect Alexander Jackson Davis lay out a gated residential park on the slope of Orange Mountain, the first planned garden suburb in the country.

title: Seneca Village Cleared
text: Seneca Village, a settlement of about 225 people founded by free Black landowners, and the other homes on the park site are cleared as construction of Central Park begins.

title: The Greensward Plan
text: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux win the Central Park design competition; the first section opens to skaters that December.

title: Draft Week
text: In July 1863 violent disturbances shake Lower Manhattan, the culmination of working-class discontent with the new law drafting men to fight in the Civil War.

title: The First Elevated
text: Charles T. Harvey's West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway demonstrates a cable-hauled elevated line above Greenwich Street; regular service begins in 1870.

title: New York Crosses the Harlem
text: The city annexes the Westchester towns of Kingsbridge, West Farms and Morrisania, the western Bronx.

title: The Els Go Uptown
text: The Sixth Avenue elevated opens in 1878, followed by the Third Avenue line; steam trains reach Harlem by 1880 and open upper Manhattan to building.

title: Brooklyn Bridge
text: The East River bridge opens after fourteen years of work; its 1,595-foot span is the longest in the world.

title: Statue of Liberty
text: Liberty Enlightening the World is dedicated on Bedloe's Island in 1886, a gift of the people of France to the United States.

title: Brooklyn Fills Kings County
text: Brooklyn, a city since 1834, spreads over the farms of Kings County. In 1894 it annexes Flatbush, Gravesend and New Utrecht, and Flatlands in 1896.

title: The World Building
text: The New York World Building on Park Row, 309 feet high, is the first building to rise above Trinity's spire. It stands until 1955.

title: Harlem River Ship Canal
text: The canal through the northern tip of Manhattan opens, cutting Marble Hill off from the island; eleven days earlier the city annexed the Bronx east of the Bronx River.

title: Greater New York
text: New York, Brooklyn, western Queens County, Staten Island and the Bronx are consolidated into one city of five boroughs and 3.4 million people.

title: University Heights
text: The domed Gould Memorial Library crowns the Bronx campus of New York University above the Harlem River; the colonnade of the Hall of Fame for Great Americans curves beside it.

title: Ellis Island
text: Ellis Island opened as an immigration station in 1892 and was enlarged with fill from about 3 to 27 acres; its main building is finished in 1900. Some twelve million people enter here by 1954.

title: Flatiron Building
text: The 22-story Fuller Building is completed on the triangle at 23rd Street, and is soon known by its shape.

title: Williamsburg Bridge
text: The second East River bridge opens with the longest suspension span in the world, 1,600 feet.

title: The Subway
text: The Interborough Rapid Transit opens from City Hall to 145th Street and Broadway, 9 miles and 28 stations.

title: Singer Tower
text: The 612-foot Singer Building becomes the world's tallest building in 1908, passed a year later by the 700-foot Metropolitan Life tower. The Singer is demolished in 1968.

title: Queensboro Bridge
text: The cantilever bridge over Blackwell's Island opens Queens to Manhattan; the Manhattan Bridge follows at the end of the year.

title: Pennsylvania Station
text: The Pennsylvania Railroad opens its station by McKim, Mead & White with tunnels under the Hudson and East rivers. It stands until 1963.

title: Grand Central Terminal
text: The new terminal opens over two levels of electrified tracks; the covered rail yard to the north becomes Park Avenue.

title: Woolworth Building
text: The 792-foot Woolworth Building opens, the tallest building in the world until 1930.

title: Black Tom
text: German agents blow up the munitions depot on Black Tom Island at the Lehigh Valley Railroad's piers. The blast breaks windows across Manhattan and scars the Statue of Liberty.

title: Hell Gate Bridge
text: The New York Connecting Railroad's steel arch, the longest in the world at 977 feet, opens between Queens and Wards Island.

title: Bronx River Parkway
text: A landscaped motor road in a cleaned-up river valley opens from the Bronx to Kensico Dam, the first parkway of its kind. Westchester builds its other parkways on its model.

title: Coney Island
text: The Wonder Wheel (1920) and the Cyclone roller coaster (1927) stand beside the boardwalk and the beach, the amusement district of the Brooklyn shore.

title: Holland Tunnel
text: The first mechanically ventilated vehicle tunnel under the Hudson opens between Canal Street and Jersey City.

title: Staten Island's Bridges
text: The Goethals Bridge and the Outerbridge Crossing open to New Jersey, the first road bridges to Staten Island.

title: The Race for the Sky
text: 40 Wall Street and the Chrysler Building rise within months of each other. The Chrysler reaches 1,046 feet in 1930, and the Empire State Building will pass it a year later.

title: Chrysler Building
text: The 1,046-foot Chrysler Building opens as the tallest building in the world.

title: Empire State Building
text: The 1,250-foot Empire State Building opens; it is the world's tallest building until 1970.

title: George Washington Bridge
text: The Hudson River bridge opens to traffic with a 3,500-foot span, nearly twice the previous record.

title: Rockefeller Center
text: The RCA Building opens in 1933 at the centre of a complex of fourteen buildings built between 1930 and 1939.

title: Triborough Bridge
text: Robert Moses's complex of three bridges joins Manhattan, the Bronx and Queens across Randalls and Wards islands.

title: Lincoln Tunnel
text: The first tube opens between Weehawken and Midtown, its looping approach cut into the Palisades. A second tube follows in 1945 and a third in 1957.

title: The World of Tomorrow
text: The World's Fair opens on Flushing Meadows, until then the Corona ash dumps, around the Trylon and Perisphere; the Bronx-Whitestone Bridge opened the day before.

title: LaGuardia Airport
text: New York Municipal Airport opens to airlines on filled land at North Beach in Queens.

title: Stuyvesant Town
text: The first tenants move into Metropolitan Life's Stuyvesant Town, built over eighteen blocks of the Gas House District.

title: Fresh Kills
text: The city begins filling the tidal marsh of Fresh Kills on Staten Island with refuse; it grows into the largest landfill in the world before closing in March 2001.

title: Idlewild
text: New York International Airport opens on the marshes of Jamaica Bay; it is renamed for John F. Kennedy in December 1963.

title: Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel
text: The longest continuous underwater road tunnel in North America opens between the Battery and Red Hook.

title: United Nations
text: The General Assembly Building opens beside the Secretariat (1950), completing the United Nations headquarters on eighteen acres of former slaughterhouses at Turtle Bay.

title: Last Train on Third Avenue
text: The Third Avenue elevated, the last in Manhattan, closes south of 149th Street and is pulled down.

title: Cross Bronx Expressway
text: The first sections of Robert Moses's expressway open. Cut through built-up neighbourhoods and displacing thousands of residents, the road is finished across the borough in 1963.

title: Tappan Zee Bridge
text: The New York Thruway crosses the Hudson at its widest point, between Nyack and Tarrytown, and opens Rockland County to the suburbs.

title: Ebbets Field
text: The Brooklyn Dodgers win the 1955 World Series, their first, and leave for Los Angeles after 1957. Ebbets Field in Crown Heights is demolished in 1960.

title: The First Container Ship
text: Malcom McLean's converted tanker Ideal X sails from Port Newark with 58 trailer boxes on deck. Within two decades the piers of Manhattan and Brooklyn stand empty.

title: Lincoln Center
text: President Eisenhower breaks ground for Lincoln Center on the cleared blocks of San Juan Hill; Philharmonic Hall opens in September 1962.

title: Penn Station Demolished
text: Demolition of Pennsylvania Station begins; Madison Square Garden opens on the site in 1968.

title: The 1964 World's Fair
text: A second World's Fair opens at Flushing Meadows around the Unisphere, which still stands. Shea Stadium, home of the Mets, opens beside it the same year.

title: Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge
text: The bridge across the Narrows opens with the world's longest suspension span, 4,260 feet, tying Staten Island to the rest of the city.

title: The Landmarks Law
text: Mayor Robert F. Wagner Jr. signs the law creating the Landmarks Preservation Commission, a response to losses like Penn Station.

title: Co-op City
text: The first residents move into Co-op City in the northeast Bronx; with 15,372 apartments it is the largest cooperative housing development in the world.

title: World Trade Center
text: The Port Authority dedicates the World Trade Center; the 110-story twin towers are briefly the tallest buildings in the world.

title: The Fiscal Crisis
text: Despite large cutbacks and mass firings of city workers, New York almost defaults in October 1975. A Municipal Assistance Corporation and an Emergency Financial Control Board are formed to deal with the crisis.

title: Battery Park City
text: The 92 acres of Battery Park City landfill, made partly from the World Trade Center excavation, are completed in the Hudson in 1976; the first apartments open in 1982.

title: The Meadowlands
text: Giants Stadium opens in 1976 beside the new racetrack on filled marsh at East Rutherford, the centrepiece of the state's plan for the Hackensack Meadowlands; the arena follows in 1981.

title: One Court Square
text: The Citicorp Building rises beside the Queens Plaza subway lines in Long Island City, a tower of the 1980s that becomes the tallest building in Queens.

title: September 11
text: Hijacked airliners destroy the twin towers; most of the 2,977 victims of the day's attacks die here.

title: Yankee Stadium
text: The new Yankee Stadium opens in April 2009 across the street from the old one, which is demolished the following year.

title: The High Line
text: The first section of the park on the disused West Side freight viaduct opens between Gansevoort and 20th streets.

title: Barclays Center
text: The Barclays Center arena opens at the junction of Atlantic and Flatbush avenues in Brooklyn in September 2012.

title: Hurricane Sandy
text: A record storm tide of nearly 14 feet at the Battery floods the shores of all five boroughs, subway tunnels and the power network; more than forty people die in the city.

title: One World Trade Center
text: One World Trade Center opens at 1,776 feet, the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

title: Second Avenue Subway
text: The first phase of the Second Avenue Subway opens with stations at 72nd, 86th and 96th streets.

title: A New Tappan Zee Bridge
text: The first span of the Governor Mario M. Cuomo Bridge opens beside the bridge of 1955, which is taken down by 2019.

title: Hudson Yards
text: The first phase of Hudson Yards opens on a platform over the West Side rail yard.

title: The City Today
text: An estimated 8.58 million people live in the five boroughs in July 2025, down from 8.80 million in the 2020 census. The harbour Hudson entered in 1609 is still the centre of the city.
